audit_notes: The shear-lag model is physically consistent: the silicone coating acts as a membrane (E_c*t_c) bonded to a rigid epoxy substrate through a shear compliance per unit area c_s = 1.5*t_c/E_c (half the coating thickness in shear, G = E/3 for incompressible silicone) + t_i/G_i (tie zone). Decay length sqrt(E_c*t_c*c_s) = 0.37 mm, domain 3 mm, so the far end is load-free. Peak interfacial shear at the cut edge tau = u(0)/c_s = sigma_0*t_c/sqrt(E_c*t_c*c_s) (for a long domain) = about 41 kPa for 50 kPa edge membrane stress. Key finding: the coating's own shear compliance (4.5e-10 m/Pa) is about 400 times the graded zone's (1.2e-12) and 22,000 times an abrupt epoxy tie-coat's (2e-14), so in this model the graded zone changes the peak interfacial stress by only about 0.1 %. The benefit claimed in the concept (removal of the bimaterial free-edge stress singularity, Dundurs mismatch of about 4 orders of modulus) exists only in a 2D elasticity model near the corner and is not represented here; the result must therefore be read as 'no benefit in the shear-lag sense', not as a disproof. Structural limits: 41 kPa interfacial shear is far below the cohesive strength of silicone (about 1-5 MPa) and typical silicone-tie-coat adhesion (0.3-1 MPa), so fender rubbing at this level does not delaminate either design. Baseline: conventional abrupt tie-coat of 20 um with shear modulus 1 GPa. abrupt_tie_layer_thickness and substrate_youngs_modulus do not enter the equation.
